name: Fatima Baker

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI firms, employers, unions, political parties or government. We sell nothing and campaign for no side. Your answers are confidential, so tell me what you would say publicly and what you actually think. What is a normal day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I’m Fatima, 58, a junior developer at a tech company making software for apartment repair requests. I came from housing-office work and earned a two-year college diploma; I still have to ask a senior to check complex fixes. I read tenant reports, test the route to the maintenance crew, and call a housing clerk when a lift request disappears. I use AI every day for test drafts, but I check building numbers and tenant details myself.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How does your job fit your household?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner Ellis maintains public parks, and our children are grown. This developer job pays well despite my junior title, and Ellis has steady hours. We have ten months of expenses saved, a mortgage, and plenty of similar jobs nearby. Retirement is in sight, but we have not verified what income or assets would actually cover the mortgage if we stopped.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the team AI Plateau changes little about a tenant needing a lift fixed. A closed repair ticket cannot carry a wheelchair up four flights.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I feel secure about my wage and Ellis’s park hours. Ten months saved also lets us handle an unexpected lift in our own building, if the owners bill us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d keep matching AI-drafted tests with the tenant’s request and the crew’s actual visit. I’d continue saving 400 each month while both wages hold. In the first year I’d keep asking a housing clerk to confirm when a lost repair request is really closed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm about our income and the mortgage. I still get angry when a tenant is told a repair happened but no one came.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which repair was closed too early?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A resident reported the only lift was stuck for two days. Our system marked it done because a contractor had accepted the job, not completed it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you give children money?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ellis and I would keep helping our grown children with occasional meals when they visit. We would not promise them money against a retirement figure we have not checked.

say: I expect **AI Plateau** to leave tenant repairs needing human confirmation.
I would check **actual crew visits** before closing lift requests.
think: I expect **both wages** to stay secure while the team still needs human repair checks.
Our **ten-month reserve** can handle an ordinary housing bill without touching the mortgage.
do: **Match** AI tests to tenant requests and completed crew visits.
**Ask** housing clerk to confirm lost requests before closure.
feel: **Calm** about household income, frustrated by false repair closure.
S0.quote: A closed repair ticket cannot carry a wheelchair up four flights.
fieldNote: Her **daily AI use** is grounded in tenant records, actual visits and housing-clerk confirmation.
Higher pay, **ten months saved** and Ellis’s steady hours support calm.

steps.text: Keep matching lift requests to actual crew visits with housing-clerk confirmation
Save 400 monthly while both wages hold

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell colleagues Steady Disruption can write and check repair code before robots maintain parks. I would ask the staff union and tenant council together to demand a named person when a lift repair is disputed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think a company might stop replacing junior developers, then narrow my role. My pay looks safe this year. A ten-month cushion does not make poor tenant records acceptable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d join a union and tenant-council meeting this month with five false-closure cases, removing names and flat numbers. I’d keep my paid testing work and ask management to report how many complaints were reopened after an AI closure. In the first year, if my hours fall, I’d apply to actual local housing-software posts only when their stated pay covers our mortgage with Ellis’s usual wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about pressure on junior roles and angry about tenants losing a human route. My own pay is secure for now, so I can press the issue openly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you bring to the joint meeting?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: One resident rang three times after a lift ticket closed itself. I would use that case without their name to ask who is accountable for the fourth call.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would Ellis’s work stay secure?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ellis’s park work is hands-on, though the scheduling may change earlier. I would not tell him his job is safe forever because robots arrive slowly.

say: I expect **Steady Disruption** to reach repair code before park robots.
I would demand **named human responsibility** for disputed lift repairs.
think: I expect **junior hiring** could slow, though my pay holds now.
I fear **false closures** could bury tenant complaints.
do: **Join** union and tenant-council meeting with five anonymised cases.
**Keep** paid repair testing and request reopened-complaint figures.
**Apply** if hours fall only to real local posts with mortgage-covering combined pay.
feel: **Uneasy** about junior roles, with own wage secure now.
S1.quote: A ten-month cushion does not make poor tenant records acceptable.
fieldNote: Her **joint group action** uses anonymised closure cases and requests a report on reopened complaints.
Her own **pay appears safe** this year, while junior hiring and tenant recourse worry her.

steps.text: Join union and tenant-council meeting with five anonymised lift cases
Keep paid repair testing and request reopened-complaint counts
Apply if hours fall only to real posts whose pay with Ellis’s usual wage covers mortgage

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell colleagues AGI by 2028 could do our repair-code thinking work in 2028, while hands-on park robots follow around 2031. Ellis’s scheduling may change earlier than his work on the ground.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think my junior post could disappear, even with a good record. Ten months saved gives us time to search, but nearby software firms might also use AGI instead of hiring.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d ask for written redundancy terms and keep the reserve available for our mortgage. I’d ask the union to press as a group for a tenant appeal route after code staff are cut. In the first year after 2028, if dismissed, I’d apply to real paid openings and eligible income help rather than assume Ellis’s wage covers everything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about my wage, but I can pay bills while we look for a real opening. I am more frightened of a city full of closed repair tickets with no one to call.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the children need to help?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the children we can handle some months, not promise endless support. Their wages belong in their own budgets.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could housing appeals replace your job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would check whether the housing office still employs people to hear disputes. A job advert is useful only if it states paid hours and the office is actually hiring.

say: I expect **2028 AGI** to reach repair code before 2031 park robots.
I would demand **tenant appeals** after coding cuts.
think: I expect my **junior post** could disappear.
I cannot assume **nearby software firms** will keep hiring after AGI.
do: **Request** written redundancy terms and reserve mortgage cash.
**Organise** union demand for tenant appeals after code cuts.
**Apply** for real paid openings and eligible help if dismissed after 2028.
feel: **Anxious** about wage loss, with ten months to search.
S2.quote: Ten months saved gives us time to search, but nearby software firms might also use AGI instead of hiring.
fieldNote: Her **strong reserve** supports a real job search but does not guarantee code vacancies after 2028.
She joins **collective appeal demands** after possible coding cuts and treats public help as eligibility-dependent.

steps.text: Organise union demand for human tenant appeals after coding cuts
Apply to real paid openings if dismissed after 2028
Apply for eligible income help if dismissed after 2028

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say AGI by 2031 reaches repair code in 2031, with hands-on park robots around 2034. Five years could let me learn to inspect whether a building is actually accessible, but I would check paid demand first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I still expect code jobs to shrink. I know the difference between a closed lift ticket and a working lift, but an inspection certificate would not guarantee a job after full thinking AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d ask two building firms for actual paid accessibility-inspector vacancies and the required supervised field hours. I’d take a course only if firms have real paid vacancies, it has supervised field practice, costs no more than 500 from discretionary savings, and leaves nine months of expenses untouched. In the first year after 2031, if coding ends, I’d apply only to actual field openings with a wage that covers our mortgage with Ellis’s usual pay, while checking whether 2034 robots are replacing inspectors.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about losing code pay, but able to risk a bounded course if the field really hires. I will not call a classroom certificate a new wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would field practice add?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At one block, the lift worked but its door closed before a walker could get through. I would need supervised field practice to measure that, not just read a diagram.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you fund training?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ellis and I would compare the inspection wage with his ordinary paid hours. We would not use our mortgage reserve to pay for an expensive course.

say: I expect **2031 AGI** to reach code before 2034 park robots.
I would check **paid inspection demand** before buying training.
think: I expect **code jobs** to shrink when full thinking AI reaches apartment software.
I cannot assume **inspection certification** guarantees a paid post after AGI or before robots.
do: **Check** two firms for paid inspector vacancies and supervised field requirements.
**Train** only with real vacancies, field practice, cost no more than 500 and nine months’ savings untouched.
**Apply** if coding ends after 2031 to real field posts with combined mortgage-covering pay despite robots.
feel: **Anxious** about code pay, with room for a bounded course.
S3.quote: I will not call a classroom certificate a new wage.
fieldNote: Her **inspection course** is capped at 500 from discretionary cash, preserving nine months of expenses.
A **field job** depends on real vacancies, supervised practice, family-covering pay and continuing demand after 2031.

steps.text: Take supervised accessibility course only for real vacancies, at most 500, with nine months saved
Apply after 2031 coding loss only to real field vacancies with combined mortgage-covering pay despite robots

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell colleagues AGI by 2036 threatens repair code in 2036; park robots follow around 2039. A decade gives workers time to bargain for paid transitions and learn what retirement actually costs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I expect my high pay to hold for several more years, though junior posts may thin out early. I will not assume a pension or our children’s wages can carry the mortgage at a date on a calendar.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d keep testing lift requests against crew visits and save 400 monthly while both wages hold. I’d bring the union yearly figures on junior hires and unresolved tenant repairs. In the first year after 2036, if my code job ends, I’d seek real paid work; I would retire only if written income, savings and mortgage figures show we can cover living costs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about younger workers and future pay, with our current mortgage secure. Ten years lets us check written numbers, not borrow a future from the children.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you verify retirement?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask our retirement providers for actual statements and compare them with the mortgage balance. We have not done that calculation yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What should the tenant council track?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The tenant council should track repairs that were reopened, not just tickets marked complete. A lift fixed on paper is still a broken lift.

say: I expect **2036 AGI** to reach code before 2039 park robots.
I would bargain for **paid transitions** and measured tenant outcomes.
think: I expect my **current wage** to hold for several years.
I cannot assume **pension or child income** covers our mortgage.
do: **Keep** checking crew visits and save 400 monthly while both wages hold.
**Bring** union yearly junior-hire and unresolved-repair figures.
**Seek** real work if dismissed after 2036; retire only with verified resources.
feel: **Uneasy** about later cuts, with current income secure.
S4.quote: A lift fixed on paper is still a broken lift.
fieldNote: She uses **tenant outcomes** and union figures during the long lead time.
The **retirement date** depends on written personal income and mortgage balances, not assumptions.

steps.text: Keep testing lift requests against actual crew visits while paid
Save 400 monthly while both wages hold

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because coding could go before workers and tenants have a plan. Written layoff terms, a real paid opening, a functioning appeal route and eligible income help would matter. Our savings buy time, not a guarantee.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask the resident whether the lift moved after the software closed the ticket. A completed form is not a completed repair.

headlineQuote: A completed form is not a completed repair.
portrait: Fatima is a **58-year-old junior developer** with a two-year diploma, high pay and ten months saved.
She uses **AI daily** on apartment-repair tests, verifying actual crew visits with housing clerks.
Her partner’s **park-maintenance hours** are steady; coding faces thinking AI before park robots.
She joins **tenant and union action** and considers capped, supervised accessibility-inspection training only against real vacancies.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could remove code work before workers and tenants have a plan.
whatWouldHelp: **Written terms**, a real paid opening, tenant appeals and eligible income help would matter.
